result.summary: Pausanias continues his tour of the victor statues at Olympia, naming boxers, wrestlers, pancratiasts and runners, their victories and their sculptors. He also digresses on the death of Chilon of Patræ, the statue of Aristotle, King Archidamus and Ergoteles of Himera.

scenes.title: Statues of victors at Olympia
scenes.summary: Pausanias walks past a row of athlete statues, giving each man's victories, home city and sculptor, with short digressions on history.

alias_notes.explanation: Surname meaning roughly 'fingertip man', from his habit of seizing opponents' fingers.

analysis.text: The passage is a catalogue of athletic fame, tying victors to their cities, teachers and sculptors, showing how Greek memory was kept in bronze and inscription.
References to Chæronea, Lamia, Antipater and Alexander date the statues to the late fourth century BC and show Macedonian power shaping Greek life.

fun_facts.text: Pausanias notes the Eleans excluded the 104th Olympiad from their records because the Pisæans and Arcadians, not Elis, had run it.

language_notes.text: Pancratiast: a contestant in the pancratium, a brutal combined boxing-and-wrestling event. 'Acrochersites' means roughly 'fingertip man', from his finger-gripping tactic.
The 104th Olympiad (364 BC) was held by the Pisæans and Arcadians, who seized Olympia from Elis; Elis later struck it from its official lists.
Amphictyonians: the league of states administering Delphi and its Pythian games, so this crown means a Pythian victory.
The sentence says the boy's statue is mentioned only because Phidias made it; its subject's identity is unknown to Pausanias.
Chæronea (338 BC) and the Lamian War (323 BC) were Greek defeats by Macedon; Pausanias dates Chilon's death by Lysippus' period.
Sepulture means burial; Archidamus died in Italy fighting barbarians and his body was not recovered.
The 'horse-trainer' is a groom or driver figure standing with the chariot group, which is dedicated by Lampus.

context_notes.text: Pythagoras of Rhegium was a famous early-fifth-century BC bronze sculptor, noted for rhythm and detail in his athletes.
The Iamidæ were an Elean family of seers, claiming descent from the prophet Iamus.
Aristotle, the philosopher, was tutor to Alexander and later enjoyed the favour of Antipater, the Macedonian regent.
Himera was a Greek city on Sicily's north coast; Ergoteles was an exile from Cretan Gnossus.

literary_notes.text: Chaining teacher to pupil (Clearchus, Euchirus, Syadra and Charta) works like a family tree, showing art passing down generations.
Pausanias speaks as a witness citing physical evidence, reinforcing his authority as a careful traveller-historian.
Pausanias appears as a rational investigator, offering a plausible explanation for a discrepancy rather than leaving it unresolved.
